urlScheme:
Legacy public datafeed (the source the owner specified). Evidence: dukascopy-node v1.46.4 src/url-generator/index.ts (https://github.com/Leo4815162342/dukascopy-node/blob/v1.46.4/src/url-generator/index.ts), its real test fixtures, and my own decoding.
Base: https://datafeed.dukascopy.com/datafeed/{SYMBOL}/{YYYY}/...
- SYMBOL is uppercase (EURUSD, GBPUSD, USDJPY, XAUUSD).
- The month folder is 0-BASED and zero-padded: 00 = January … 11 = December.
- The day is 1-based and zero-padded (01..31). The hour is zero-padded (00..23).
- Every bucket is a UTC period.

File types:
- 1m candles, one file per UTC day: {SYMBOL}/{YYYY}/{MM0}/{DD}/BID_candles_min_1.bi5 (ASK_candles_min_1.bi5 for ask). For example, …/EURUSD/2024/00/15/BID_candles_min_1.bi5 is 2024-01-15.
- 1h candles, one file per UTC month: {SYMBOL}/{YYYY}/{MM0}/BID_candles_hour_1.bi5
- 1d candles, one file per UTC year: {SYMBOL}/{YYYY}/BID_candles_day_1.bi5
- Ticks, one file per UTC hour: {SYMBOL}/{YYYY}/{MM0}/{DD}/{HH}h_ticks.bi5 (20-byte records).
- There is no month-level 1m file in the scheme. The only monthly file holds hourly candles, so one month of 1m data takes 28–31 daily requests. I could not probe this live.

How I verified the 0-based month (empirically):
- The fixture at path …/2019/01/ (hourly) has 672 records = 28 days, which is February 2019.
- The fixture at …/2019/00/ has 744 records = 31 days, which is January.
- …/2019/01/05/BID_candles_min_1.bi5 is a full trading day (Tue 2019-02-05), not Saturday 2019-01-05.

Successor JSON API, used by dukascopy-node 1.49.0 and later (2026-07-16):
- The library builds the host from character codes (src/config/data-api.ts), which deliberately hides it.
- Host and path: https://jetta.dukascopy.com/v1/candles/minute/{CODE}/{BID|ASK}/{YYYY}/{M}/{D}. Month and day are 1-based and unpadded. CODE looks like 'EUR-USD' or 'XAU-USD'.
- Other paths: /candles/hour/{CODE}/{PRICE}/{YYYY}/{M}, /candles/day/{CODE}/{PRICE}/{YYYY}, /ticks/{CODE}/{YYYY}/{M}/{D}/{H}. The bucket that contains 'now' uses ?from=<epoch ms>.
- The response is delta-encoded JSON {timestamp, multiplier, shift, open/high/low/close, times[], opens[], highs[], lows[], closes[], volumes[]}. Minutes without ticks are left out (src/data-normaliser/index.ts on master).
- This API is undocumented and now sits behind a WAF (see httpBehavior).
httpBehavior:
MEASURED HERE (2026-10-18 15:44 UTC, Windows, curl 8.21/Schannel):
- TCP connects to datafeed.dukascopy.com (16.62.244.190, an AWS address), but the TLS handshake is reset: 'Recv failure: Connection was reset', curl exit 35. www.dukascopy.com behaves the same way. https://example.com works from the same shell.
- The WebFetch service also got ECONNRESET for www.dukascopy.com pages, so the cause may not be local.
- I tried two follow-up diagnostics: a TLS server-name (SNI) test and a Node fetch HEAD. The session's permission classifier denied both as 'Containment Escape', and I tried no other route to Dukascopy.
- So I could not measure live: status codes for empty or future days, response headers, or rate limits.

DOCUMENTED / REPORTED BEHAVIOR:
(1) The bi5 datafeed has been broken since 2026-07-07 (dukascopy-node issue #254, https://github.com/Leo4815162342/dukascopy-node/issues/254):
- The reporter wrote: "The TLS handshake completes successfully, but the server never sends any response body".
- Other users saw mostly timeouts and 503s, including from several VPN locations.
- The maintainer wrote: "It seems like dukascopy has changed the datafeed and underlying APIs".
- On 2026-07-17 a tester on PR #257 reported the old endpoint "still timed out".
(2) The successor JSON API is blocked for scripts:
- It returned HTTP 429 rate limits in July 2026.
- Since 2026-10-16 it has returned an AWS WAF challenge: HTTP 202, 'x-amzn-waf-action: challenge', server CloudFront, content-length 0, no Retry-After.
- This reproduced with Node fetch, Python urllib, curl, wget and curl_cffi impersonating Chrome. Only a headed Chrome browser succeeded (issue #261, opened 2026-10-17, https://github.com/Leo4815162342/dukascopy-node/issues/261).
- With retryCount 0, a challenged request silently looks like an empty dataset.
(3) Empty bodies on the old feed:
- No-data buckets came back as 200 with 0 bytes; weekend tick hours, for example, were empty files (Tickstory and MQL4 forum reports).
- Empty bodies also happened transiently. That is why dukascopy-node has retryOnEmpty: "requests with successful but empty (0 Bytes) responses should be retried" (https://www.dukascopy-node.app/config/node).
- Its test suite models 'no data' as a 0-byte empty.bi5.
- 404 was reported for files that do not exist, such as dates before an instrument's start.
- Future days: unverified. The importer should never request anything after yesterday (UTC).
(4) Headers: dukascopy-node sent no custom headers at all (a bare fetch(url) in src/buffer-fetcher/index.ts) and worked for years. So no browser User-Agent or Referer was needed for the bi5 feed, and changing headers does not get past the 2026 WAF.
(5) Throttling:
- dukascopy-node defaults to batches of 10 parallel requests with a 1 s pause, documented as "Main purpose - not to fall under rate limiting restrictions".
- Tickstory support blamed bulk-download failures on throttling (2018), and 503s on Dukascopy's weekend maintenance.
recordLayout:
Verified on five real Dukascopy files (see testsDone).

LZMA header (13 bytes, 'LZMA alone' format):
- Props byte 0x5D: lc=3, lp=0, pb=2.
- dictSize, uint32 little-endian: 0x00400000 (4 MiB).
- Uncompressed size, uint64 little-endian. It is always KNOWN: 34,560 for a minute file, 17,856 for a 31-day hourly file, 8,760 for a 365-day daily file.
- There is NO end-of-stream marker, and the decoder consumes the input exactly to the last byte.

Payload: N records of 24 bytes each, big-endian:
- int32 timeOffsetSeconds
- int32 OPEN
- int32 CLOSE
- int32 LOW
- int32 HIGH
- float32 volume
The price order is O, C, L, H, not OHLC.

Time base is the start of the file's UTC bucket:
- Minute files: 00:00 UTC of that day. Offsets run 0..86340 in steps of 60, always 1,440 records.
- Hourly files: 00:00 UTC on the 1st of the month, 24 records per calendar day.
- Daily files: 1 Jan 00:00 UTC, 365 or 366 records.
- Absolute time = bucketStartUtc + offset.

Price = int / 10^digits.

Proof of field order:
- Across all 4,661 records, only two assignments satisfy H >= max(O,C), L <= min(O,C) and H >= L for every record: field 3 = low, field 4 = high, with fields 1 and 2 being open and close in either order.
- The continuity check next.open == prev.close then decides it. Fields 1/2 as open/close: 689/1439 and 682/1439 minute pairs match. The reverse: 93 and 101. So field 1 = open and field 2 = close.
- This matches dukascopy-node v1.46.4: src/decompressor/index.ts (5× readInt32BE plus readFloatBE in a 24-byte struct) and src/data-normaliser/index.ts ("const [sec, open, close, low, high, volume] = values;", time = sec*1000 + startTs).

Volume:
- It is a float32 liquidity figure (EURUSD minute volumes ranged 1.5–1291.9 on the test days).
- Use it only to detect flats (volume == 0), then drop it, since the output format is [t,o,h,l,c].

Ticks (not needed for this work): 20 bytes = int32 ms offset, int32 ask, int32 bid, float32 askVol, float32 bidVol.

priceScales.evidence: Verified on real data: the 2019-02-04 file's ints span 114244..114603, which is 1.14244..1.14603 (EURUSD traded around 1.143-1.146 that day); the 2019-02-05 file spans 1.14011..1.14404. dukascopy-node v1.46.4 src/utils/instrument-meta-data/generated/instrument-meta-data.json has decimalFactor 100000. Minute data starts 2003-05-04 21:00 UTC.
Same metadata file: decimalFactor 100000, minute data from 2003-05-04. Not checked against a real GBPUSD file (none available).
Same metadata file: decimalFactor 1000, minute data from 2003-05-04. Not checked against a real file.

Same metadata file: name XAU/USD 'Spot gold', decimalFactor 1000, minute data from 2003-05-05. Not checked against a real file. The importer should sanity-check that the decoded price is in a plausible range for the date (e.g. 1,500-5,000) on the first file of each run. Note: dukascopy-node v1.50.0 removed decimalFactor because the JSON API sends a 'multiplier' with each response; bi5 still needs this table.

weekendBehavior:
Every bucket is present in the file. Minute files always have 1,440 records, hourly files have 24 per calendar day including weekends, and daily files have 365/366 records including Saturdays. A period with no ticks is a 'flat': O=H=L=C = previous close, volume 0.

Verified on the real files:
- All 214 zero-volume hours in January 2019 and all 192 in February 2019 are flat and carry the previous close.
- Those zero-volume runs are exactly Fri 22:00 → Sun 21:00 UTC (48 h, winter time) every weekend, plus New Year's Day 2019 from 00:00 to 21:00 UTC.
- On the two EURUSD weekdays, 0 of 2,880 minutes had volume 0.
- In the 2019 daily file, the only zero-volume days are the 52 Saturdays. 2019-12-25 has about 5% of normal volume.
- dukascopy-node's docs say flats come mostly from 'weekends and bank holidays' (ignoreFlats, default true).

NOT verified (no file available):
- A Saturday minute file. Expected: 1,440 flats.
- The summer offset. Expected: open/close at 21:00 UTC, i.e. 17:00 New York.
- Gold's daily break. Expected: about 1 h of flats around 17:00–18:00 New York.
- Weekend tick-hour files are reportedly 0 bytes.

CLOSED vs MISSING:
Inside a file the two look identical (zero-volume flats), so the importer has to decide using each symbol's market-hours config: weekly session defined in America/New_York (Sun 17:00 → Fri 17:00 for FX), daily breaks, and holidays.
- Zero-volume minutes inside a closed window: drop silently.
- Zero-volume runs during open hours: drop them, but report them per day (e.g. runs of 5 minutes or more) as 'no ticks during session'.
- Treat these as missing or corrupt: a fully flat day that should be open; a 0-byte or 404 response for an open day; an LZMA error; a header size other than 34,560; offsets other than i×60; OHLC violations; volume 0 with unequal prices. Retry with backoff, then report, and leave that month incomplete so the next run retries it. Also flag spikes using a per-symbol threshold on |close/prevClose − 1|.
- Saturdays can be skipped for FX and gold.

TYPICAL COUNTS (non-flat 1m candles):
- FX weekday: 1,440.
- Sunday: ~120 in winter, ~180 in summer.
- Friday: ~1,320 in winter, ~1,260 in summer.
- Saturday: 0.
- About 30–32k per FX symbol per month. Gold has about 60 fewer per weekday (daily break), so about 30k per month.
- Raw records in the files per month = days × 1,440 (e.g. 44,640 for a 31-day month).
lzmaOptions:
(a) Vendored pure-JS decoder — RECOMMENDED. I built and tested a prototype:
- File: C:\Users\kadir\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\c--Users-kadir-OneDrive-Masa-st--Wawe-Journal-astro\97ee93d7-3b56-4094-909f-8a419fcb57d4\scratchpad\agents3\dukascopy-scripts\lzma-alone.mjs. It is 180 lines / 7.7 KB, ESM, with no dependencies.
- I wrote it from the LZMA specification, which is part of the public-domain LZMA SDK ('LZMA SDK is placed in the public domain.' https://www.7-zip.org/sdk.html; the SDK's reference decoder is LzmaSpec.cpp). There is no licence obligation, so it can go into scripts/lib/ as our own code.
- Structure:
  - Header parse: props → lc/lp/pb, dictSize, 64-bit size (all 0xFF means unknown).
  - Range decoder: first byte must be 0, then a 4-byte code; 11-bit adaptive probabilities with move-shift 5; normalise when range < 2^24; direct bits for large distances.
  - Probability models: isMatch / isRep0Long per 12 states × posState; isRep / isRepG0-2 per state; literal coders 0x300×2^(lc+lp), with the 'matched literal' path when state ≥ 7; two length decoders (choice / low 3-bit / mid 3-bit / high 8-bit); 6-bit posSlot trees per lenState; reverse trees for special distances; 4-bit align tree.
  - Main loop: literal; match (new distance, rep0..3 shift, end marker = 0xFFFFFFFF); short rep; rep0–rep3 long reps.
  - Output: kept fully in memory as the window, with strict checks: distance < pos and < dictSize, output length equals the declared size, and truncated input throws.
- Test method (test-lzma.mjs in the same folder):
  - Decode each fixture and compare byte-for-byte with `xz --format=lzma -dc`.
  - Round-trip synthetic buffers (empty, 1 byte, text, zeros, random, synthetic candles and flats) through xz presets -0/-1/-6/-9e and several lc/lp/pb/mf/nice variants, each also with a 'known size' header patch.
  - Round-trip through Python's lzma FORMAT_ALONE as an independent encoder.
  - Truncations and bit flips must throw.
- Result: 152/152 passed. All 9 truncations and all 400 bit flips threw.
- Speed: about 3.9 ms per daily file (8.5 MB/s), so about 40 s of CPU for the whole backfill.
- For the repo's node --test, commit tiny vectors generated by xz from synthetic data, not Dukascopy files (their terms forbid redistribution).
- LZMA has no checksum, so always validate the payload as well.

(b) Spawning xz:
- Works here (Git Bash xz 5.8.3, `xz --format=lzma -dc`).
- Not present on stock Windows or macOS, needs one process per file (~10k spawns), and adds an external binary. Use only as a dev cross-check.

(c) Built-in route: none.
- Node v25.2.1 zlib has gzip, deflate, brotli and zstd only.
- DecompressionStream accepts gzip, deflate, deflate-raw and brotli; 'lzma' and 'xz' throw TypeError (I checked).
- The npm package the old dukascopy-node used (lzma-purejs-requirejs) is excluded by the no-npm rule.

Note: the successor JSON API needs no LZMA at all.
recommendation:
Do NOT build the forex/gold archive on Dukascopy until the owner clears two blockers.

(1) ACCESS:
- The specified bi5 datafeed has been unresponsive since 2026-07-07 (dukascopy-node #254).
- Its undocumented JSON successor has answered every non-browser client with an AWS WAF bot challenge since 2026-10-16 (#261). Only a headed Chrome browser gets through.
- From this machine even the TLS handshake to *.dukascopy.com is reset.
- So a plain Node script cannot rely on Dukascopy today. Solving or replaying the WAF challenge would mean getting around an access control, so I advise against it.

(2) LICENCE:
- Dukascopy's Terms of Use limit downloads to "your own personal, non-commercial use".
- They forbid using the site's information "to construct a database of any kind" and forbid distributing or displaying it without written agreement.
- A shared archive in Supabase Storage served to app users (Wawe Journal has payments) is exactly that, so it needs Dukascopy's WRITTEN permission.

OWNER ACTION:
- Ask Dukascopy for a data licence that covers an access method and display to app users.
- Otherwise choose a forex/gold source whose licence allows display to app users. That needs its own evaluation; I did not research alternatives.
- Crypto from Binance (another track) is unaffected.

IF permission and a working endpoint are obtained, build a 'dukascopy' source adapter like this:
- Download one BID_candles_min_1.bi5 per UTC day (0-based month folder). Only complete days up to yesterday (UTC); skip Saturdays.
- Decode with the vendored decoder. Header size must be 34,560; read the 24-byte big-endian records (O, C, L, H order); drop flats (volume 0).
- Validate, and classify gaps against the market-hours config.
- Write UTC rows [t, o, h, l, c] rounded to 5/5/3/3 decimals into monthly .json.gz files.
- Resume by listing Storage, plus a per-symbol manifest (month status and gap report) and a git-ignored local raw cache.
- Network: concurrency 2 (at most 4); a 30 s timeout via AbortSignal.timeout; exponential backoff with jitter on 429, 5xx, timeouts and 0-byte bodies (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 s; honour Retry-After; 6 attempts).
- Pause for 10 minutes after 5 consecutive failures. Treat 202 + x-amzn-waf-action as a hard stop, never as empty data. Avoid weekends (maintenance).
- Send an honest User-Agent with a contact address.
- Keep the source behind an adapter interface so Binance and any future forex source write the same format.
volumeEstimate:
Range: 2020-01-01 to 2026-10-17, the last complete UTC day (today, 2026-10-18, is a Sunday). That is 2,482 days (1,773 weekdays, 354 Sundays, 355 Saturdays) across 82 months.

Requests:
- Daily 1m files: 2,482 × 4 symbols = 9,928 requests.
- 8,508 if Saturdays are skipped (they are all flats for FX and gold).
- Afterwards, about 105–124 requests per month for 4 symbols.

Download size:
- Real EURUSD weekday files are 11,582 B and 11,568 B.
- Flat or partial days are about 2–3 KB (estimated from synthetic flats compressed with xz: 1.75–1.96 KB).
- Total about 85–90 MB. Gold may be somewhat larger, so budget up to 150 MB.
- Decoded data is about 327 MB (34,560 B per day per symbol), processed as a stream.

Duration (one-off):
- Concurrency 2–4 with at least 250 ms between requests: about 15–40 min.
- A cautious 1 request/s: about 2.4 h.

Output estimate (from real decoded candles):
- 44.5 B per row as JSON; gzip -9 brings it to 8.2 B per row.
- About 1.36 MB JSON, or about 250 KB .json.gz, per FX symbol-month (~32k rows).
- About 80 MB for 4 symbols × 82 months.

- "Except written agreement between you and DUKASCOPY, you agree to use the WEBSITE solely for your own non-commercial use and benefit". An exact-phrase search confirms this wording.
- "Such download is licensed to you by DUKASCOPY ONLY for your own personal, non-commercial use in accordance with the TCU and does not transfer any other rights to you."

- "The WEBSITE and the information contained therein may not be used to construct a database of any kind." FXMacroData quotes the same sentence in an article dated 2026-10-05 (https://fxmacrodata.com/articles/fxmacrodata-vs-dukascopy-historical-data).
- A search excerpt of the same page: "You may not copy, reproduce, … distribute, publish, display, … create derivative works from, transmit, or in any way exploit any part of the WEBSITE".

Dukascopy Europe Terms of Use (https://www.dukascopy.com/europe/english/legal-pages/terms-of-use/): the same personal, non-commercial clause. According to the search summary, it also bans storing site content in databases and automated scraping or data mining without written consent.

report:
DUKASCOPY TRACK — findings (2026-10-18)

BOTTOM LINE
- The bi5 format is fully specified and verified on real files, and a no-npm LZMA decoder is built and tested.
- Even so, Dukascopy is NOT a usable automated source today, and its terms forbid what we want to do.
- The specified bi5 datafeed has been reported dead since 2026-07-07 (https://github.com/Leo4815162342/dukascopy-node/issues/254). The maintainer's comment there: "dukascopy has changed the datafeed and underlying APIs".
- The reference library moved to a hidden JSON API (jetta.dukascopy.com/v1, v1.49.0 on 2026-07-16). That API has answered scripted clients with AWS WAF challenges since 2026-10-16: HTTP 202, x-amzn-waf-action: challenge (https://github.com/Leo4815162342/dukascopy-node/issues/261, opened yesterday).
- From this machine the TLS handshake to datafeed.dukascopy.com and www.dukascopy.com was reset, while example.com worked.
- Dukascopy's Terms of Use allow downloads only for personal, non-commercial use and ban building a database or redistributing without written agreement.
- So the owner must get Dukascopy's written permission and a working access method, or pick another forex/gold source. Binance crypto is unaffected.

WHAT I COULD NOT DO, AND WHY
- I planned up to 6 GETs and a few HEADs against datafeed.dukascopy.com, to measure status codes for weekend, empty and future days, headers and rate limits.
- The first request failed at TLS (connection reset).
- My next two diagnostics were denied by the auto-mode permission classifier as 'Containment Escape': an SNI test pointing the Dukascopy hostname at another IP, and the same URL via Node fetch. I made no further attempt to reach Dukascopy.
- Live HTTP behaviour is therefore taken from documentation and issue reports, not measured.
- Completing those probes would need the user to allow this session's network access to dukascopy.com, or someone to run them from a network where Dukascopy is reachable. Given #254 and #261 they would likely fail anyway.
- DEVIATION TO NOTE: to still verify the record layout empirically, I downloaded 5 small real Dukascopy files from GitHub instead of from Dukascopy. They are the test fixtures that dukascopy-node v1.46.4 commits under src/__mocks__ (Dukascopy datafeed files for EURUSD; their git blob hashes match the repo tree). I treated them as untrusted data: only decoded, never executed. There was no GBPUSD, USDJPY or XAUUSD fixture, so those scales come from the library's instrument metadata.

FORMAT (verified)
- URL: https://datafeed.dukascopy.com/datafeed/{SYM}/{YYYY}/{MM 0-based, 2 digits}/{DD}/BID_candles_min_1.bi5, one file per UTC day.
- Hourly candles: /{SYM}/{YYYY}/{MM0}/BID_candles_hour_1.bi5. Daily candles: /{SYM}/{YYYY}/BID_candles_day_1.bi5. Ticks: /{DD}/{HH}h_ticks.bi5.
- There is no monthly 1m file.
- File: LZMA-alone. Header 0x5D, 4 MiB dictionary, KNOWN uncompressed size (34,560 = 1,440 × 24), no end marker.
- Records: 24 bytes big-endian = int32 seconds from 00:00 UTC of the file's day, int32 open, int32 CLOSE, int32 LOW, int32 HIGH, float32 volume.
- I proved the order with an OHLC-consistency permutation test plus an open/close continuity test, and it agrees with dukascopy-node's decompressor and normaliser.
- Scales: EURUSD 1e5 (verified on data), GBPUSD 1e5, USDJPY 1e3, XAUUSD 1e3 (from dukascopy-node metadata).
- Every minute, hour and day is present in the files. Closed periods are flats: O=H=L=C = previous close, volume 0. Verified: weekends Fri 22:00 → Sun 21:00 UTC in winter, New Year's Day 2019, Saturdays in the daily file; no zero-volume minutes on normal weekdays.
